title: Why Are You Afraid?
paragraphs:
Why Are You Afraid?
The Question That Exposed the Storm Inside the Disciples—and the Storm Inside Us
The waves were real.
The wind was real.
The danger was real.
The fear was real.
Yet the most shocking part of the story was not the storm.
It was the question Jesus asked afterward.
"Why are you afraid?"
For many people, that question almost feels unfair.

After all, the disciples were not imagining things. They were not overreacting. They were not creating drama. They were trapped in a violent storm on the Sea of Galilee. Experienced fishermen believed they were about to die.
But Jesus asked the question anyway.
And perhaps that is because His question was never really about the storm around them.
It was about the storm within them.
The account appears in multiple Gospel narratives, but Matthew records it with striking clarity:
"Then He arose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. But He said to them, 'Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?'" (Matthew 8:26).
The Greek text preserves the force of Jesus' words:
"Τί δειλοί ἐστε, ὀλιγόπιστοι;" (Ti deiloi este, oligopistoi?)
Literally:
"Why are you cowardly, you of little faith?"
The word "δειλοί" (deiloi) is stronger than simple nervousness. It describes a fear that overwhelms trust. A fear that forgets who is present.
Jesus was not condemning human emotion.
Scripture never teaches that fear itself is sin.
Again and again, God's people experienced fear.
David experienced fear.
Elijah experienced fear.
Jeremiah experienced fear.
Even in Gethsemane, Jesus experienced deep anguish.
The issue was not that the disciples felt afraid.
The issue was that they allowed fear to become larger than the One who was in the boat with them.
That is why this story still pierces the human heart thousands of years later.
Because most of us are not drowning in Galilee.
We are drowning somewhere else.
Some are drowning in debt.
Some are drowning in anxiety.
Some are drowning in loneliness.
Some are drowning in grief.
Some are drowning in regret over sins they cannot seem to forget.
Some are drowning in shame from scandals they hope nobody ever discovers.
Some are drowning in questions they cannot answer.
Some are drowning in prayers that seem unanswered.
And when the waves keep crashing, we often ask the same question the disciples asked:
"Lord, don't You care?"
But the Gospel reveals something astonishing.
Before the disciples ever questioned Jesus, Jesus already knew the storm was coming.
He intentionally entered the boat.
He intentionally crossed the sea.
He intentionally allowed them to experience what appeared to be impossible circumstances.
Nothing surprised Him.
Nothing caught Him off guard.
Nothing threatened His sovereignty.
The disciples saw chaos.
Jesus saw an opportunity to reveal His glory.
That truth becomes even more powerful when viewed through the Hebrew understanding of faith.
The Hebrew word often associated with faith is "אֱמוּנָה" (emunah).
Emunah is not merely believing that God exists.
It is steadfast trust.
Faithfulness.
Dependability.
A settled confidence in God's character even when circumstances appear contradictory.
The disciples believed Jesus could perform miracles.
But at that moment they struggled to trust Him while the storm was still raging.
And if we are honest, so do we.
We trust God when the diagnosis is negative.
Can we trust Him when the diagnosis is positive?
We trust God when money is abundant.
Can we trust Him when the account is nearly empty?
We trust God when relationships are flourishing.
Can we trust Him when hearts are breaking?
This is where the story stops being about fishermen and becomes about us.
Because every believer eventually discovers that faith is easy in calm waters.
Faith becomes visible in storms.
And yet the most beautiful detail in the entire account is often overlooked.
Jesus was sleeping.
Not because He was indifferent.
Not because He lacked compassion.
Not because He was unaware.
He slept because He possessed perfect confidence in His Father's sovereignty.
The storm that terrified the disciples never threatened the peace of Christ.
Think about that.
The same storm that convinced the disciples they were dying failed to disturb the rest of Jesus.
What if the peace we desperately seek is not found in the absence of storms?
What if true peace is found in the presence of Christ?
The Gospel repeatedly points us toward that reality.
The world's definition of peace is the removal of problems.
The biblical definition of peace is the presence of God.
The Hebrew word "שָׁלוֹם" (shalom) means far more than the absence of conflict.
It describes wholeness.
Completeness.
Restoration.
Harmony with God.
The disciples wanted the storm removed.
Jesus wanted their faith strengthened.
They wanted survival.
He wanted transformation.
And that is often how God works in our lives.
The storm you wish would disappear may be the very place where God intends to reveal Himself most clearly.
Not because He enjoys your suffering.
Not because He delights in pain.
But because He loves you too much to leave your faith shallow.
The cross itself proves this.
The darkest day in human history became the greatest demonstration of divine love.
What looked like defeat became victory.
What looked like tragedy became redemption.
What looked like scandal became grace.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
From Eden to Calvary to the empty tomb, God has been rewriting impossible stories.
Peter the failure became Peter the preacher.
Paul the persecutor became Paul the apostle.
The woman caught in adultery received mercy.
The thief on the cross received paradise.
Broken people became redeemed people.
Lost people became found people.
Scandal became grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Perhaps that is why His question remains so powerful.
"Why are you afraid?"
Not because storms are imaginary.
Not because suffering is insignificant.
Not because pain is easy.
But because the One asking the question is the same One who conquered death.
The One who commands the wind.
The One who commands the sea.
The One who carries scars that purchased our redemption.
The One who promised:
"Lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." (Matthew 28:20)
If Christ is in the boat, the storm does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe today your greatest fear is not financial.
Not physical.
Not emotional.
Maybe your deepest fear is that your failures have disqualified you from God's love.
If so, hear the Gospel clearly.
The cross declares otherwise.
Your sin is not greater than His grace.
Your shame is not greater than His mercy.
Your past is not greater than His redemption.
Your scandal is not greater than His power to rewrite your story.
That is why Jesus came.
That is why He died.
That is why He rose again.
And that is why His question still echoes through every generation:
"Why are you afraid?"
Because when Jesus is present, fear no longer gets to sit on the throne.
Christ does.
If this message stirred your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
What storm has God been teaching you through lately?
Your testimony may become someone else's lifeline.
Together, we can reach more hearts with biblical truth, grace, hope, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
One day you will realize the storm was never sent to destroy you—it was the place where you finally saw who was in the boat.
